This design hits on a few things that I struggle with:
1. Passthrough apis, that pass through one protocol to another.  These are difficult to authenticate/authorize/test well, and add dependencies into the chain.
2. APIs not backed by a standard or specification (OpenBMCs history of adoption of these is spotty).
3. Protocols that are functionally closed to change (ipmi).
4. New features that already have an implementation.  IPMI works just fine over the http-dbus-rest protocol that has existed for a long time.  SOL already works fine over a websocket without needing RMCP overhead.  I'm certain there's improvements here, but we need to articulate those with testing/numbers so that we can tell folks when to use each tool, and to make sure that maintaining two implementations is worth it.

In the ideal, the ipmi spec could have a new definition for "ipmi over http" that we could implement, but as we know, the ipmi specification has been abandoned by it's owners, so this is functionally just an openbmc OEM interface, even though this design doc makes it appear as a normal interface.  This design needs to make it clear in external naming that this is OpenBMC OEM defined, and has really nothing to do with "IPMI" at a protocol layer, aside from sharing some command sets.
+ @alexander@amelkin.msk.ru as the owner of ipmitool maintainer.

As an alternative that accomplishes the same goal, could we please look at implementing http-connect support?

https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9298

The advantages are:
1. In theory no changes to ipmitool are required.  (ipmitool would've needed to add an http + websocket dependency for this design).  We could just proxy UDP RMCP using a side application, which would mean that ANY ipmi enabled tool could now work.  If ipmitool wanted to implement http-connect directly, it would reduce the required dependencies a bit (we'd only need HTTP, not websocket implementations).
2. All network protocols are governed by specifications.  This gives maintainers a way to make sure things are correct without needing to nit pick every item or be an expert on network protocols.
3. it clearly delineates responsibilities between applications.  bmcweb is responsible for authenticating, and tunneling UDP packets.  IPMI is responsible for IPMI specification correctness.  In the model proposed here, bmcweb is responsible for assembling correct ipmi commands, which is something the webserver shouldn't be responsible for.
4. It's more likely to be generically useful in other situation.  Http-connect would let us proxy.... anything, not just IPMI.
5. Far more HTTP and UDP experts have reviewed and understand the http-connect protocol than we will get here.  That likely reduces the chance for protocol level CVE events.

The http connect protocol on top of HTTP seems pretty trivial.  Open the http request, authenticate using headers, then it's just 16 bit length and udp.  An initial implementation could write only to ipmi if we wanted to.

The idea of this doc is not only to use `https` as the network layer, but more importantly to replace the RMCP authentication.

We want to get rid of lanplus so that BMC will not be required to store password at all.

> Passthrough apis, that pass through one protocol to another. These are difficult to authenticate/authorize/test well, and add dependencies into the chain.

This design is expected to introduce a new "pass through" API just like net-ipmid. The handler is ipmid and it is ipmid who is responsible to handle the raw data correctly.

> APIs not backed by a standard or specification (OpenBMCs history of adoption of these is spotty).
> Protocols that are functionally closed to change (ipmi).

This is proposed as OpenBMC extension to ipmi.

> New features that already have an implementation. IPMI works just fine over the http-dbus-rest protocol that has existed for a long time. SOL already works fine over a websocket without needing RMCP overhead.

There is no `ipmitool` support, this design is to extend the capability for ipmitool to use the "modern" protocol with minimal impact and still keep the performance as lanplus.
Indeed it coulb be implemented by "not changing OpenBMC" at all and just change `ipmitool` to use the REST API, but:
1. REST API is going to be deprecated (and it exposes the whole DBus)
2. It has worse performance compared to lanplus.

So this design introduces the `/ipmi` websocket with binary data protocol. It aims to provide a minimal change but competitive performance.

> We want to get rid of lanplus so that BMC will not be required to store password at all.

That's fine, the above can still accomplish that goal.  IPMI supports network modes where the password/user isn't used at all.  Would still like to see your thoughts on the above.

net-ipmid isn't a passthrough API, net-ipmid only implements the protocol

> This is proposed as OpenBMC extension to ipmi.

IPMI as a specification doesn't have a provision for protocol extensions, so I'm not really sure what this means.  This would be a completely new protocol, that's essentially ipmi remoted over a websocket.

> REST API is going to be deprecated 

I'm not really sure what this means, and it's just that nobody uses that protocol because it's a passthrough API.

> It has worse performance compared to lanplus.

Citation and example needed.  When you provide results, please make sure you've enabled HTTP2.

I am not sure how to provide the citation, it's manually built bmcweb with HTTP2 enabled, and tested with the same ipmi command.

For the `http-connect` way, I see several questions about the "advantages":

> In theory no changes to ipmitool are required

The goal is to "bypass" lanplus, I do not see the appropriate "interface" in existing ipmitool that could be used to connect to the http-udp tunnel.

Do you propose which existing interface could be used here?

> All network protocols are governed by specifications.

This is the same as the proposal of this patch.

> bmcweb is responsible for authenticating, and tunneling UDP packets. IPMI is responsible for IPMI specification correctness. In the model proposed here, bmcweb is responsible for assembling correct ipmi commands, which is something the webserver shouldn't be responsible for.

As mentioned above, I do not see which existing interface could be used.
Btw, in my proposal, bmcweb does "minimal" assembling of ipmi commands. It's basically a bridge between websocket's binary data and D-Bus data.

Why not Redfish as an alternative ? 
Why instead of taking IPMI doing something it was never designed for? Why not just use Redfish?

Using redfish to replace ipmi is the way to move forward.
But ipmi is heavily used for management in data centers, and it's not easy to "switch" from ipmi to Redfish in the near future.

As OpenBMC already introduces "DBus" interface to ipmitool, this doc introduces "https" interface as well.

> But ipmi is heavily used for management in data centers, and it's not easy to "switch" from ipmi to Redfish in the near future.

I'm not following why this design helps that though, versus just including the relevant capabilities in Redfish.  Which features were Redfish missing compared to ipmitool, and why was implementing those features not an alternative.

Overall, I'm not in support of this from a maintenance and security perspective.  IPMI as a standard has no new versions, and despite some continued use is deprecated by its creators.  We need to heed that deprecation as a good reason to not continue to extend.  IF there were an IPMI consortium still, this would almost certainly be rejected.

ipmitool is one tool of many in the ipmi landscape.  While implementing support for ipmitool for this interface is great, it doesn't bring the whole industry worth of tooling over to using this new interface, and without a lot of critical mass behind this, I worry a lot about the maintenance aspects including testing that this feature will find.

This design doc would be helped a lot by articulating what ipmi use cases are missing from the openbmc redfish implementation, so we can get them added.

I'd also add that if this is truly what's desired there's already a way to do this over the dbus-rest option, but the lack of use seems to me that there's not widespread desire for this.

If this is still something you want to pursue, the things that would convince me that this should be included in openbmc are:
1. A number of contributors asking for this, testing patches, and providing input.
2. A defined mechanism for how we handle security for something that has no specification, or tie this design to an existing http proxy specification
3. Articulating why (at a protocol level) that the existing http request/response mechanisms can't be made more performant without external interface changes.
4. Articulating the use cases that Redfish doesn't have that IPMI requires.

If you feel like I'm wrong here, please feel free to avail yourself of the technical oversight forum, which can likely offer other input.
Submitted https://github.com/openbmc/technical-oversight-forum/issues/52 for TOF discussion.

The "beauty" of CVE-2013-4786 is that the attacker doesn't even need the rootfs access to get the password hash, it can be extracted directly from communicating with the BMC, not even by a MitM attack.

However, that is mitigated administratively by putting the BMC into a trusted network environment and by prohibiting any unauthorized external access to that environment.

IMO, there is no need in introducing any new access interfaces to a legacy protocol.

> The "beauty" of CVE-2013-4786 is that the attacker doesn't even need the rootfs access to get the password hash, it can be extracted directly from communicating with the BMC, not even by a MitM attack.

Exactly, that's something this design proposed to replace the lanplus protocol.

> IMO, there is no need in introducing any new access interfaces to a legacy protocol.

This is something I would like to discuss in TOF. Although it's a legacy protocol, it's used a lot in our data centers, and that's why the https interface is introduced.
